ABSTRACT
Coal possesses a dense, cross-linked structure and strong π - π stacking interactions that hinder activator pene -
tration and cause excessive graphitization, which limits its application in zinc-ion hybrid capacitors (ZIHCs). 
Herein, we propose a synergistic deep eutectic solvent (DES) swelling and in-situ air carbonization strategy to 
fabricate defect-rich, heteroatom-doped porous carbon from raw coal. Utilizing the ZnCl
2
-H
3
PO
4 
DES, the non- 
covalent interactions of coal are disrupted, which significantly increases its fraction of free volume from 16.29% 
to 31.45% to facilitate deep activator penetration. During the subsequent air carbonization, the DES functions as 
a condensed-phase flame retardant to prevent over-burning, alongside serving as an in-situ activator and P 
dopant. The in-situ formation of thermally stable C-O-C bridge bonds introduces spatial steric hindrance that is 
proposed to promote a local hybridization shift from sp
2 
toward sp
3 
carbon. This effectively inhibits the tight 
stacking of aromatic sheets and suppresses excessive graphitization. The optimized carbon is characterized by a 
greatly disordered structure, a high specific surface area, rich sp
3
-C defective sites, a hierarchical pore structure, 
and P/N co-doping. Benefiting from these structural composition merits, the assembled flexible ZIHC with a 
ZnCl
2
-PVA gel electrolyte achieves a specific capacity of 248 mAh g
� 1 
alongside an energy density of 174 Wh 
kg
� 1
. The synergy of DES swelling and in-situ activation offers a sustainable, efficient route for coal-based porous 
carbon, with potential to extend to diverse precursors for structurally and compositionally rich carbon materials.
1. Introduction
Benefiting from their high safety, low cost, and fast charge transport 
kinetics, zinc-ion hybrid capacitors (ZIHCs) have attracted extensive 
research attention as potential energy storage candidates [ 1 ]. Due to 
their excellent electrical conductivity, tunable pore structures, and su -
perior electrochemical stability, porous carbons are widely utilized as 
cathode materials in ZIHCs [ 2 ]. Because the cathode crucially dictates 
the capacity and rate performance of ZIHCs, rationally designing porous 
carbon cathodes featuring both hierarchical porous channels and a 
highly active interface is important [ 3 ].
Coal serves as a cost-effective and carbon-rich precursor that con -
tains a 3D network. In this network, aliphatic chains and ether linkages 
connect polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and strong π - π 
stacking interactions also exist [ 4 ]. While such a highly aromatic 
structure endows coal-derived carbons with outstanding intrinsic con -
ductivity and structural stability, the tightly cross-linked matrix and 
potent intermolecular forces severely impede the diffusion of activators 
[ 5 ]. Consequently, the derived carbon materials often suffer from 
inhomogeneous pore evolution and constrained specific surface areas. 
Moreover, high-temperature carbonization in an inert atmosphere cau -
ses intense condensation and aromatization in PAH-rich coal [ 6 ]. This 
process preferentially produces highly graphitized carbons that lack 
structural defects and reactive sites. This highly ordered lattice config -
uration fails to offer adequate Faradaic charge compensation, thus 
severely limiting the overall electrochemical performance [ 7 ].

Pretreatment to dissociate the macromolecular structure of raw coal 
is a reliable method to prepare high-performance coal-based porous 
carbon [ 8 ]. The swelling method has aroused considerable attention due 
to its user-friendly procedures and mild conditions. Through the pene -
tration of swelling agents, this method effectively disrupts the 
non-covalent interactions within the coal macromolecular network, 
promotes the volume expansion of coal, and achieves the dissociation of 
its cross-linked structure [ 9 ]. Commonly used swelling agents mainly 
include organic solvents [ 10 ] and ionic liquids (ILs) [ 11 ]. Among them, 
despite becoming a research hotspot because of their high polarity and 
eco-friendly nature, the high cost of ILs severely restricts their 
large-scale applications. In contrast, emerging deep eutectic solvents 
(DESs) possess the advantages of ILs while offering lower cost and 
environmental friendliness [ 12 ]. Wang et al. [ 13 ] designed a novel 
FeCl
3
-levulinic acid (LA) DES and utilized it as a bifunctional agent for 
the microwave-assisted swelling and catalytic pyrolysis of Naomaohu 
coal. During the swelling stage, this DES effectively disrupts the weak 
chemical bonds between coal layers and enlarges the interlayer spacing. 
In the subsequent pyrolysis stage, it exerts a highly efficient catalytic 
effect. Yang et al. [ 14 ] systematically compared the swelling effects of 
ChCl-glycerol, ChCl-levulinic acid, and FeCl
3
-LA DESs against tradi -
tional organic solvents on Naomaohu coal. The study demonstrated that, 
compared to traditional solvents which barely alter the coal structure, 
DES swelling pretreatment not only removes impurities such as Ca
2 +
and 
Mg
2 +
but also significantly reconstructs the microstructure of coal 
(evidenced by an increased d
002 
and a decreased L
a
), thereby dramati -
cally enhancing its pyrolysis reactivity. Based on this remarkable 
structural reconstruction effect of DESs on coal, researchers in recent 
years have further extended the DES swelling strategy to the fabrication 
of high-performance coal-based porous carbons. Our team conducted a 
series of studies based on a K
2
CO
3
-ethylene glycol (EG) DES system [ 15 ]. 
In this system, EG serves to swell the Kuche coal network and break 
bridge bonds, while K
2
CO
3 
acts as an in-situ activator during carbon -
ization. Using this dual swelling-activation advantage, 3D inter -
connected porous carbon via direct carbonization was fabricated. On 
this basis, our team also introduced an acid-regulation strategy to pre -
cisely tailor the defects and pores. The optimized coal-based carbon 
possessed abundant defects and oxygen functional groups, achieving a 
significantly enhanced specific surface area of 1304 m
2 
g
� 1 
and a 
gravimetric capacitance of 353 F g
� 1 
[ 9 ]. However, current DES pre -
treatments can only deconstruct the cross-linked network of raw coal. 
Since the subsequent carbonization is generally still performed in an 
inert atmosphere, the high aromaticity of PAHs continues to drive them 
through a typical liquid-phase carbonization process, ultimately trans -
forming them into highly graphitized carbon materials.
In addition to our previous work on coal swelling, we have carried 
out pioneering research via a flame-retardant-facilitated synthesis of 
porous carbons under an air atmosphere. We successfully achieved the 
fabrication of porous carbons derived from coal tar pitch [ 16 ] and 
biomass [ 17 ] in air. For instance, we used montmorillonite (MMT) as a 
gas and condensed-phase flame-retardant functional agent to prepare a 
series of highly defective porous carbons from coal, biomass, and 
polymers via a one-step oxidative carbonization method in air. MMT 
acted as both a flame retardant and a template, and the C-O-C bonds 
introduced in air effectively suppressed the liquid-phase carbonization 
of CTP, ultimately forming a defect structure dominated by sp
3
-C [ 18 ]. 
Similarly, we also adopted a K
2
CO
3
-KCl molten salt system acting as a 
bifunctional flame retardant and an activator to successfully achieve the 
direct carbonization of blended coal in air. The K
2
CO
3
-KCl not merely as 
a condensed-phase flame retardant to hinder the carbon skeleton from 
burning but also exhibited excellent activation and pore-forming capa -
bilities. Consequently, a coal-based porous carbon was obtained 
featuring a high specific surface area of 2380 m
2 
g
� 1 
and superior 
capacitive performance (374 F g
� 1
) [ 19 ]. In view of this, rationally 
designing a multifunctional system that integrates swelling, 
high-temperature flame retardancy, and activation in air emerges as an 
innovative approach for the customized design of highly defective, 
high-surface-area coal-based porous carbons, thereby enabling superior 
electrochemical energy storage.
This work proposes an integrated strategy to fabricate coal-based 
porous carbons with hierarchical pores and abundant defects via 
ZnCl
2
-H
3
PO
4 
DES-induced swelling of Heishan coal, followed by in-situ 
oxidation and carbonization in air; the novelty is that one single DES 
realizes the integration of coal swelling, in-situ activation, and flame 
retardancy in an air-atmosphere process. During the swelling pretreat -
ment stage, the DES can deeply penetrate the coal, break its intermo -
lecular bond interactions in the coal, disrupt the dense structure, and 
reduce the cross-linking degree of the coal. During the subsequent air 
carbonization stage, ZnCl
2 
and H
3
PO
4 
act as condensed-phase flame 
retardants and in-situ activating agents. This effectively prevents the 
excessive burning of the carbon skeleton in air and creates spatial steric 
hindrance via the evolution of C-O-C bonds. This changes the carbon -
ization path of coal, inhibits excessive graphitization, and ultimately 
yields the carbon materials characterized by high specific surface area, 
abundant sp
3
-C defects, and moderate P/N heteroatom-doped electro -
chemical active sites. Furthermore, ZnCl
2 
was used to formulate ZnCl
2
- 
PVA gels that were assembled with the synthesized porous carbons into 
flexible ZIHCs, and the resulting devices exhibited superior electro -
chemical performance.

3. Results and discussion
As shown in Fig. S1 , H
3
PO
4 
shows a distinct characteristic absorption 
peak at ~1143 cm
� 1
, which is assigned to the P
–

ZnCl
2
, this characteristic peak undergoes a significant redshift to 
~1125 cm
� 1
. This shift is attributed to strong coordination between 
Zn
2 +
and H
3
PO
4
, confirming the formation of the DES [ 20 ]. Further -
more, DSC and Raman characterizations also demonstrate the successful 
synthesis of DES ( Fig. S2 ). Fig. 1 a illustrates the preparation process of 
coal-based porous carbon, which involves swelling pretreatment of coal 
using a DES, followed by direct carbonization in air. During the swelling 
process, the DES penetrates into the pores of the coal, effectively dis -
rupting non-covalent interactions and this process induces volumetric 
expansion of the coal, transforming its originally dense structure into a 
looser state ( Fig. S3 ). During the subsequent carbonization stage in air, 
H
3
PO
4 
acts as a condensed-phase flame retardant, and it forms a pro -
tective layer on the coal surface that isolates coal from oxygen and in -
hibits excessive loss of the carbon skeleton. ZnCl
2 
serves as a chemical 
activator to etch the carbon skeleton. The final product is a porous 
carbon co-doped with P and N atoms. The XRD patterns in Fig. 1 b show 
that raw coal and DES-swelling coal retain diffraction peaks at ~26
◦
which correspond to the carbon (002) plane, and this confirms that the 
swelling process does not disrupt the carbon skeleton of the coal. 
Notably, the sharp SiO
2 
peak in the swollen coal is significantly weak -
ened ( Fig. 1 b). This may be attributed to the swelling-induced expansion 
and rearrangement of the coal macromolecular network, which re -
distributes the originally aggregated SiO
2 
and partially re-embeds them 
within the coal matrix [ 21 ]. Such structural expansion also opens in -
ternal diffusion channels within the coal, which facilitate the uniform 
penetration of subsequent activators. As depicted in Fig. 1 c, FT-IR 
spectra show that, compared to raw coal, the -OH peak (~3400 cm
� 1
) 
of the swollen coal is enhanced, indicating that DES disrupts the coal's 
hydrogen-bond network, leading to the enhancement of -OH groups 
[ 22 ]. The intensified band of the -CH
3 
located between 2800 and 
3000 cm
� 1 
suggests that swelling leads to the exposure of aliphatic side 
chains following the relaxation of the coal's macromolecular network.
